title: Poach One Chicken: Ginger-Scallion Chicken, Rice, and a Pot of Broth
description: Poach one bird gently with ginger and scallion and it does three jobs: sliced chicken over broth-cooked rice tonight, pulled meat for a second dinner, and about 3 quarts of broth. One 4-pound chicken, three meals.
notes: Buy the smallest whole chicken you can find; a 4-pound bird gives about 1 1/2 pounds of cooked meat, and the gentle poach keeps even the breast moist. Serve two-thirds of the meat tonight and pull the rest off the bones for a noodle soup or fried rice later in the week. Soy sauce can replace the tamari but adds wheat, and the ginger-scallion oil keeps for a week in the refrigerator. Refrigerate the chicken and broth within 2 hours of cooking; cool the broth quickly by setting the pot in a sink of cold water. Cooked chicken keeps 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, and the broth keeps 4 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen in quart containers. Reheat chicken and broth to 165°F before serving.

ingredients.name: whole chicken (about 4 lb / 1.8 kg), giblets removed
fresh ginger (3-inch piece), half thinly sliced and half finely grated
kosher salt, plus 1 teaspoon for the rice and oil
jasmine rice (370 g), rinsed until the water runs clear
english cucumber, thinly sliced, for serving

instructions: Fill an 8-quart stockpot with 4 quarts of water and add the sliced ginger, 4 of the scallions cut into 2-inch lengths, the smashed garlic, and 1 tablespoon of salt. Bring to a boil over high heat.

Lower the chicken into the pot breast side up; the water should cover it, so add more hot water if it does not. Return the pot to a bare simmer, with only a few bubbles breaking the surface, then cover and cook at that gentle simmer for 20 minutes.

Turn off the heat and leave the pot covered for 30 minutes. Check the thickest part of a thigh with an instant-read thermometer; it must read 165°F. If it is short, return the pot to a simmer for 5 to 10 minutes and check again.

While the chicken rests in the pot, ladle 3 cups of the poaching broth into a medium saucepan, add the rinsed rice and 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and bring to a boil. Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 15 minutes, then let it stand off the heat, still covered, for 10 minutes.

Make the ginger-scallion oil: thinly slice the remaining 4 scallions and put them in a small heatproof bowl with the grated ginger and 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Heat the neutral oil in a small skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers, about 2 minutes, then pour it over the scallions; it will sizzle. Stir in the tamari.

Lift the chicken onto a cutting board and let it rest 10 minutes. Remove the legs and breasts, slice two-thirds of the meat for tonight, and pull the rest off the bones into a container for a second dinner. Season the sliced chicken with a little salt and pepper.
Return the carcass and bones to the pot and simmer, uncovered, for 45 to 60 minutes to deepen the broth. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer; you should have about 3 quarts.
Serve the sliced chicken over the rice with spoonfuls of ginger-scallion oil, cucumber slices, and a small cup of hot broth on the side.

title: Mexican-Style Arroz con Pollo with Chicken Thighs and Peas
description: Chicken thighs browned and simmered into tomato-tinted rice with peas and carrots. One pound of thighs feeds six because the rice does the heavy lifting, about $2 a plate.
equipment: 12-inch skillet or 5-quart Dutch oven with lid
notes: Rinsing the rice keeps the grains separate instead of gummy, so do not skip it. The chicken is only browned at first and finishes cooking in the rice; check that a piece reads 165°F before you serve. Boneless chicken breast works in place of thighs but dries out more easily, so cut it into larger 1 1/2-inch pieces. The jalapeño is mild once seeded; leave it out for small children or add a second one for heat. Leftovers keep 4 days in the refrigerator and freeze well for 3 months in portions; refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking. Reheat with a splash of water, covered, until steaming and 165°F throughout.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs (450 g), cut into 1-inch pieces
long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed

instructions: Toss the chicken with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, the cumin, and the chili powder. Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet with a lid over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Add the chicken in a single layer and cook without moving it for 2 to 3 minutes, until browned on one side, then stir and cook 1 minute more. It will not be cooked through yet. Transfer to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the onion, and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and jalapeño and cook 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes so every grain is coated in oil and the edges turn translucent.

Stir in the tomato sauce, broth, and the remaining 1 teaspoon of salt and bring to a boil. Nestle the chicken and any juices into the rice, cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 18 minutes without lifting the lid.

Scatter the peas and carrots over the top without stirring, cover again, and cook 5 minutes more. Turn off the heat and let the pan stand, covered, for 5 minutes. The liquid should be absorbed, the rice tender, and the chicken should read 165°F.
Fluff with a fork, taste for salt, and finish with black pepper, cilantro, and lime wedges at the table.

title: Polish-Style Unstuffed Cabbage with Ground Turkey and Rice
description: All the flavor of gołąbki without the rolling: ground turkey and rice simmered with a whole head of cabbage in tomato sauce. One pound of turkey feeds six because the cabbage costs about a dollar.
notes: A small, heavy head of cabbage is the one to buy; it will look like too much in the pot but collapses to a third of its volume. Ground beef (85% lean) can stand in for the turkey; it then needs to reach 160°F rather than 165°F. Using neutral oil in place of the butter and skipping the sour cream makes the dish dairy-free. If you have dried marjoram, add a teaspoon with the thyme, as a Polish cook would. The stew thickens as it sits; loosen leftovers with a little broth or water when reheating to 165°F. Refrigerate within 2 hours; it keeps 4 days in the refrigerator and 3 months in the freezer, and tastes better on day two.

ingredients.name: small head green cabbage (about 2 lb), cored and cut into 1-inch pieces
long grain white rice (140 g), rinsed

instructions: Melt the butter in a 6-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the turkey and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, breaking it into small crumbles with a wooden spoon, for 6 to 7 minutes until no pink remains. Scoop it into a bowl, leaving the fat behind.
Add the onion and carrot to the pot and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes until softened. Stir in the garlic, paprika, and thyme and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the cabbage in two or three handfuls with the remaining 1 teaspoon of salt, stirring each addition until it wilts enough to make room, about 5 minutes total.
Return the turkey to the pot and add the rice, crushed tomatoes, tomato sauce, broth, brown sugar, vinegar, bay leaf, and pepper. Stir well and bring to a boil.
Cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring once or twice and scraping the bottom, until the rice is tender and the cabbage is soft. The turkey should read 165°F.
Turn off the heat and let the pot stand, covered, for 10 minutes so the rice finishes absorbing the sauce. Remove the bay leaf and taste for salt and vinegar.
Ladle into bowls and top each with a spoonful of sour cream and a pinch of dill.

title: Dal Keema: Spiced Ground Beef with Red Lentils and Peas
description: A North Indian-style keema where a cup of red lentils melts into one pound of ground beef, so six eat well over rice for about $1.75 a plate. Peas and a squeeze of lemon finish it.
equipment: 5-quart Dutch oven or deep 12-inch skillet with lid
notes: Split red lentils cook down completely in about 25 minutes and thicken the keema so it mounds on the rice; brown lentils stay whole and need 40 minutes, so stick with red. Ground turkey or ground lamb work in place of the beef (turkey needs 165°F). Swap the ghee for neutral oil to make the dish dairy-free. If the pot looks dry before the lentils are soft, add water 1/4 cup at a time. This is a good freezer meal: cool, refrigerate within 2 hours, and keep 4 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen. Reheat with a splash of water, stirring, until it reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: dried split red lentils (200 g), rinsed
cooked brown or white rice, hot, for serving

instructions: Melt the ghee in a 5-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, for 6 to 8 minutes until deep golden at the edges. Stir in the ginger, garlic, and chile and cook 1 minute.
Add the beef and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, breaking it into fine crumbles, for 6 to 8 minutes until browned with no pink remaining and a thermometer reads 160°F.
Stir in the coriander, cumin, turmeric, cayenne, and 1 teaspoon of the garam masala and cook for 1 minute, until the spices smell toasted and coat the meat.

Add the lentils, crushed tomatoes, water, and the remaining 1 teaspoon of salt. Bring to a boil, then cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer for 25 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick, spoonable sauce.
Stir in the peas and the remaining 1 teaspoon of garam masala and cook, uncovered, for 3 to 4 minutes until the peas are hot. Stir in the cilantro and taste for salt.
Spoon over hot rice and serve with lemon wedges for squeezing over each plate.

title: Italian Sausage with Cannellini Beans and Kale
description: A Tuscan-style skillet where one pound of crumbled Italian sausage seasons two cans of white beans and a bunch of kale. Serve with crusty bread; about $2 a bowl for six.
notes: Hot or sweet sausage both work; if the sausage is lean, add another tablespoon of oil for the onion. Crushing a handful of the beans against the side of the pan thickens the broth without any flour. Leaving off the Parmesan makes the dish dairy-free. Chickpeas or butter beans can replace the cannellini, and spinach can replace the kale if you stir it in during the last minute. Serve over toasted crusty bread or polenta to stretch it further; that adds wheat if you use bread. Refrigerate within 2 hours; leftovers keep 4 days and reheat gently to 165°F with a splash of broth.

ingredients.name: fresh sweet or hot italian pork sausage (450 g), casings removed
cannellini beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
lacinato or curly kale (about 8 oz), stems removed and leaves torn

instructions: Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the sausage and cook, breaking it into bite-size pieces, for 6 to 8 minutes until browned and cooked through to 160°F. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon, leaving the fat in the pan.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the onion, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, red pepper flakes, and rosemary and cook for 1 minute.

Add the tomatoes with their juice, the beans, and the broth. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes, crushing about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pan with the back of a spoon to thicken the liquid.
Pile the kale on top with the salt, cover, and cook for 3 minutes until it wilts, then stir it down into the beans and return the sausage to the pan.
Simmer, uncovered, for 5 minutes until the kale is tender and the liquid has reduced to a loose, saucy consistency. Stir in the lemon juice and season with pepper and more salt to taste.
Ladle into bowls and pass grated Parmesan at the table.

title: Thịt Kho Trứng: Vietnamese Caramel-Braised Pork Shoulder with Eggs
description: Pork shoulder simmered in a bittersweet caramel with fish sauce until it nearly falls apart, with hard-boiled eggs soaking up the sauce. A pound and a half feeds six over rice, and it tastes better on day two.
equipment: 4-quart heavy pot or Dutch oven with lid
notes: Take the caramel to a deep amber, the color of iced tea, and no darker; it should taste faintly bitter, not burnt, and the water added afterward will spit, so pour it in at arm's length. Pork shoulder is the right cut because its fat keeps the meat moist through a long simmer; pork loin turns dry. Many Vietnamese cooks use coconut water in place of plain water, and you can do the same for a rounder sweetness. The eggs are the stretch: each one is half a serving, so add two more if you are feeding eight. Refrigerate within 2 hours in the sauce; it keeps 4 days, and the fat rises and seals the top. Skim or stir the fat back in and reheat to 165°F on the stove.

ingredients.name: boneless pork shoulder (680 g), cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes
serrano or green chile, thinly sliced, for serving
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: Put the eggs in a medium saucepan, cover with cold water by an inch, and bring to a boil. Turn off the heat, cover, and let stand 10 minutes, then move the eggs to a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes and peel them.
Season the pork cubes with the salt and pepper and set them near the stove.

Combine the sugar and 2 tablespoons of water in a 4-quart heavy pot over medium heat. Swirl the pot rather than stirring, and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the syrup turns a deep amber. Standing back, pour in 1/2 cup of the water; it will sputter. Stir until the caramel dissolves.
Add the pork, shallot, garlic, fish sauce, and the remaining 2 1/2 cups of water. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then partly cover and simmer over low heat for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the peeled eggs, uncover, and simmer for 20 to 30 minutes more, turning the eggs now and then so they color evenly, until the pork is fork-tender and the sauce has reduced to a thin glaze that coats a spoon.
Taste the sauce; add a little more fish sauce if it needs salt or a pinch of sugar if it tastes sharp. Serve the pork, eggs, and sauce over hot rice with scallions and chile on top.

title: Filipino Chicken Afritada with Potatoes, Carrots and Bell Pepper
description: Bone-in chicken thighs braised in tomato sauce with chunks of potato, carrot and bell pepper, so one thigh anchors a full plate for each of six. Six thighs cost about what one rotisserie chicken does.
notes: Bone-in thighs are the cheapest chicken by the pound and the bones flavor the sauce; buy a family pack and freeze the rest. Dry the skin well before browning so it crisps instead of steaming. Fish sauce gives the savory depth that Filipino cooks expect; soy sauce can replace it but adds wheat and soy. Cut the potatoes larger than the carrots so both finish at the same time, and check that the chicken reads 165°F at the bone before serving. Refrigerate within 2 hours; leftovers keep 4 days and the sauce thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when reheating to 165°F. The potatoes turn mealy if frozen, so freeze only the chicken and sauce.

ingredients.name: bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (about 2 1/4 lb / 1 kg)
russet or yukon gold potatoes (680 g), peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
red bell pepper, cut into 1-inch pieces
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: Pat the chicken thighs dry and season with 1 teaspoon of the salt and the pepper. Heat the oil in a 6-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

Lay the thighs in skin side down and cook, without moving them, for 6 to 7 minutes until the skin is deep golden. Flip and cook 3 minutes more, then transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of the fat.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the onion, and cook for 4 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic and cook 1 minute.

Add the tomato sauce, broth, fish sauce, and bay leaf and bring to a simmer, scraping up the browned bits. Return the chicken skin side up with any juices, cover, and simmer over low heat for 20 minutes.
Tuck the potatoes and carrots into the sauce around the chicken with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes until a knife slides easily into the potatoes.
Add the bell pepper and peas, and simmer uncovered for 5 minutes until the pepper is tender-crisp and the sauce has thickened slightly. The chicken should read 165°F at the bone.
Remove the bay leaf, taste the sauce for salt, and serve each thigh with vegetables and plenty of sauce over hot rice.

title: Japanese Curry Rice with Beef Chuck and Potatoes (Kare Raisu)
description: Japanese home-style curry from a homemade roux, no boxed cubes: one pound of chuck simmered until tender with potatoes, carrots and sweet cooked-down onions. A pound of beef comes to six plates for about $2.25 each.
notes: Chuck is the right cut here: it costs less than stew meat already cut up and turns tender after 45 minutes of gentle simmering, so cut it small and let the pot do the work. The grated apple and the slow-cooked onions give the mild sweetness Japanese curry is known for; a tablespoon of ketchup and soy sauce round it out. For a gluten-free version, use gluten-free tamari and thicken with 2 tablespoons of cornstarch stirred into cold water instead of the flour roux; using neutral oil in place of the butter makes it dairy-free. Boneless chicken thighs can replace the beef with a 20-minute simmer, and they must reach 165°F. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the curry keeps 4 days and thickens as it chills, so loosen it with water when reheating to 165°F. It freezes for 3 months, though the potatoes soften; scoop them out first if that bothers you.

ingredients.name: boneless beef chuck roast (450 g), trimmed and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
yukon gold potatoes (680 g), peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
japanese short-grain rice (300 g), cooked according to the package, for serving

instructions: Season the beef with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Heat the oil in a 5-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the beef in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per batch, turning once. Transfer to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium, add the onions, and cook, stirring often, for 10 to 12 minutes until soft and golden; this slow cooking is where the curry's sweetness comes from. Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook 1 minute.
Return the beef with its juices, add the broth and grated apple, and bring to a boil. Cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer for 45 minutes until the beef is nearly tender.
Add the carrots, potatoes, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Cover and simmer for 20 minutes until a knife slides easily into the potatoes and the beef is fork-tender.

While the vegetables cook, make the roux: melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium-low heat, whisk in the flour, and cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until pale golden and nutty-smelling. Stir in the curry powder, garam masala, and cayenne for 30 seconds, then take the pan off the heat.

Ladle 1 cup of hot broth from the pot into the roux and whisk until smooth, then stir the mixture back into the pot with the ketchup and soy sauce. Simmer, uncovered, stirring often, for 5 to 8 minutes until the curry is thick enough to coat a spoon.
Stir in the peas and cook 2 minutes more. Taste for salt and serve the curry spooned over the rice.

title: Cuban-Style Picadillo with Potatoes, Raisins and Capers
description: Ground beef simmered with tomato, diced potato, sweet raisins and briny capers, the Cuban weeknight classic. One pound of beef over rice and black beans feeds six for about $2 a plate.
notes: Picadillo is usually made with pimento-stuffed green olives; capers give the same briny note from the pantry, and a handful of chopped olives can go in alongside if you have them. The diced potato is what makes a pound of beef serve six, so cut it small enough to cook through in the sauce. Ground turkey works in place of beef and needs to reach 165°F instead of 160°F. Leftovers are good folded into tortillas or spooned over baked potatoes. Refrigerate within 2 hours; it keeps 4 days in the refrigerator and 3 months in the freezer. Reheat in a covered skillet with a splash of water until it reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes (450 g), peeled and cut into 1/2-inch dice
black beans (15 oz), drained, rinsed and warmed, for serving
cooked brown or white rice, hot, for serving

instructions: Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the beef and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, breaking it into small crumbles, for 6 to 8 minutes until browned with no pink remaining and a thermometer reads 160°F. Spoon off all but about 2 tablespoons of fat.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the onion and bell pepper, and cook for 5 minutes until softened. Stir in the garlic, cumin, oregano, and bay leaf and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute until it darkens a shade, then add the tomato sauce, potatoes, water, raisins, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Bring to a simmer.

Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring once, until the potatoes are tender and the sauce has thickened enough to cling to the meat. Add a splash of water if it looks dry before the potatoes are done.
Stir in the capers and vinegar, remove the bay leaf, and season with pepper and more salt to taste.
Serve over hot rice with the warm black beans spooned alongside.

title: Carolina-Style Chicken Bog with Thighs, Bacon and Rice
description: The South Carolina one-pot of chicken, rice and smoky pork cooked together until the rice is soft and the broth is nearly gone. One pound of thighs and four strips of bacon make six big bowls.
notes: A true bog is wetter than a pilaf, so do not worry if the rice looks loose when you lift the lid; it settles as it rests. Smoked sausage is the traditional pork; if you have 8 ounces, slice it and use it in place of the bacon, browning it the same way. The hot sauce at the table is part of the dish and adds no allergens. Cooked rice dishes should be cooled and refrigerated within 2 hours, and this one keeps 3 days; it also freezes for 2 months in flat bags. Reheat with a few spoonfuls of broth, covered, until steaming hot and 165°F. Check a piece of chicken with a thermometer before serving the first time; it should read 165°F.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs (450 g), cut into 1-inch pieces
long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed
louisiana-style cayenne pepper hot sauce, for serving

instructions: Cook the bacon in a 6-quart Dutch oven over medium heat, stirring, for 6 to 8 minutes until crisp. Scoop out half of it onto a paper towel for topping, leaving the rest and all the fat in the pot.

Raise the heat to medium-high. Season the chicken with 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, the pepper, and the cayenne, add it to the pot, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring once or twice, until browned at the edges.
Add the onion and celery and cook for 5 minutes until softened, then stir in the garlic and thyme and cook for 1 minute.
Add the rice and stir for 1 minute to coat it in the fat. Pour in the broth, add the bay leaf and the remaining 3/4 teaspoon of salt, and bring to a boil.
Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes without lifting the lid, until the rice is tender and most of the broth is absorbed.
Turn off the heat and let the pot stand, covered, for 10 minutes. Check that the chicken reads 165°F, remove the bay leaf, and fluff gently with a fork.
Spoon into bowls and top with the reserved bacon, scallions, and a few dashes of hot sauce.
